title: Acid–base indicators and titrations
competency: Choose an indicator, use equivalents and normality, and calculate concentrations from titration data.

en.text: An indicator is a weak organic acid HIn whose acid form and base form have different colours: HIn + H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + In⁻. In acid the equilibrium lies left (acid colour); in base it lies right (base colour). Each indicator changes colour over its own pH range, so we choose one whose range includes the pH we want to detect.

screens.text: Why does an indicator show its acid colour in strong acid?
opts: High [H₃O⁺] shifts HIn ⇌ H⁺ + In⁻ to the left
The indicator becomes a strong base
screens.ans: High [H₃O⁺] shifts HIn ⇌ H⁺ + In⁻ to the left
screens.why: Le Chatelier: added H₃O⁺ is a product, so HIn (acid colour) dominates.

en.text: One equivalent of an acid supplies one mole of H⁺; one equivalent of a base supplies one mole of OH⁻. Equivalent mass = molar mass ÷ n, where n is the number of H⁺ or OH⁻ per formula. Normality N = equivalents per litre = n × M. At neutralization, equivalents of acid = equivalents of base, so N₁V₁ = N₂V₂.

screens.title: Equivalents
paras: One equivalent supplies or reacts with one mole of H⁺ (or OH⁻).
n = H⁺ per acid formula or OH⁻ per base formula: HCl 1, H₂SO₄ 2, NaOH 1, Ba(OH)₂ 2.
Equivalent mass = molar mass ÷ n. H₂SO₄: 98 ÷ 2 = 49 g.

screens.title: Normality
paras: Normality N = equivalents of solute ÷ litres of solution.
N = n × M: 1 M H₂SO₄ = 2 N.
Equivalents = N × V (in L).
At neutralization: N₁V₁ = N₂V₂.

en.text: In a titration the titrant (known concentration) is added from a burette to the analyte with an indicator, until the indicator changes colour. The equivalence point is where equivalents of acid and base are equal; the end point is where the indicator changes colour, and a good indicator makes them match. Then C_acid = V_base × C_base ÷ V_acid.

am.text: በቲትሬሽን ቲትራንት ከቡሬት ይጨመራል፤ አመልካቹ ቀለም ሲቀይር ይቆማል። የተመጣጣኝነት ነጥብና የመጨረሻ ነጥብ መመሳሰል አለባቸው።

notes.text: p.42: in base the indicator shows its own base colour, not always "blue" (phenolphthalein turns pink).
Example 1.10 does not answer which indicator to use; suggested: bromcresol green (3.8–5.4), or litmus/methyl red to show acidity.
p.44: 1 mol H₂SO₄ is 2 equivalents (one equivalent = ½ mol = 49 g); the promised normality equation is missing (N = equivalents/V(L) = n × M).
Two examples are numbered 1.10; the normality example should be Example 1.11. "Moles of base = moles of acid" (p.45) holds only for 1 : 1 reactions.
